###### Posted on September 17, 2026


Running a hybrid event means planning two experiences at once: one for the people in the room and one for the people watching from home. A solid


**hybrid event checklist** keeps both sides organized, so the virtual side doesn’t become an afterthought. This guide walks through the 12 steps that matter most in 2026, from setting goals to measuring results after the event.


Table of Contents


Toggle


##


**What is a Hybrid Event?**


A hybrid event combines an in-person gathering with a live virtual experience happening at the same time. In-person guests get the room, the handshakes, and the free coffee. Virtual guests get a live stream, chat, and on-demand replays. Both groups take part in the same event, just through different doors.


Beyond that basic definition, hybrid events give organizers flexibility that a single-format event can’t. In-person attendees still get networking and hallway conversations. Virtual attendees can join from anywhere without travel costs. Done well, a hybrid format grows the size of an audience without growing the venue.


That interaction is the real draw, not just a side effect: in a


[Zoom-commissioned study of event marketers](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/webinars/resources/future-of-hybrid-events-report/) , 61% named the interaction between virtual and in-person attendees the single greatest benefit of running a hybrid event, ahead of cost savings.


##


How Do You Plan a Hybrid Event?


Planning a hybrid event means working through 12 steps in order: setting goals, budgeting for both audiences, understanding attendee split, choosing the right platform, planning content, staffing two teams, handling production, driving engagement, marketing to both audiences, setting up registration, managing event day, and following up afterward. Skipping steps early causes problems later.


### 1. Define Your Goals and Objectives


Every hybrid event strategy starts with knowing what the event needs to achieve before booking a venue or picking software. Lead generation, brand awareness, training, and community building all call for different formats, so name the goal first. A lead-gen event needs interactive sessions and a way to capture attendee information. A training event needs recorded sessions people can revisit later.


Write the goal down as a number where possible: a target attendee count, a lead target, or a satisfaction score from post-event surveys. A vague goal like “raise awareness” is hard to plan around and impossible to measure afterward.


### 2. Set a Realistic Budget for Both Experiences


Hybrid events run two budgets at once: an in-person budget (venue, catering, AV) and a virtual budget (streaming platform, virtual production, tech support). Start a spreadsheet with a line item for each cost, and add a buffer for anything unplanned, since AV problems and last-minute venue changes are common.


Budget Category In-Person Virtual


Venue & staging Venue rental, signage, seating N/A


Technology On-site AV equipment Streaming platform, bandwidth


Staffing Front desk, ushers Moderators, tech support


Content Speaker fees, travel Recording, editing


Contingency 10-15% buffer 10-15% buffer


Update the budget as planning moves along, and share it with stakeholders regularly so nobody is surprised by the final number.


### 3. Understand Your Audience


Hybrid events serve two distinct audiences, and they don’t want the same thing. Survey past attendees or pull data from previous events to estimate how many people will show up in person versus online.
That split changes real decisions: a mostly virtual crowd justifies spending more on streaming quality; a mostly in-person crowd shifts budget toward the venue experience.


### 4. Choose the Right Tools for Hybrid Events


The event platform is the backbone of a hybrid event, so the tools for hybrid events chosen here need to handle registration, streaming, and attendee engagement without forcing organizers to stitch together separate systems. Look for[event registration and ticketing](https://inevent.com/en/registration-forms-rsvp-invites.php) built into the same system as the live stream, so data doesn’t get lost between platforms.


Build the agenda inside the platform once you choose a tool, and make sure it clearly separates in-person sessions from virtual ones. Add buffer time between sessions for technical resets, and share the agenda with attendees ahead of time so they can plan their day.


### 5. Plan Content That Works for Both Audiences


Content needs to hold up whether someone is sitting in the third row or watching from their kitchen table. InEvent event strategists recommend building sessions with the virtual audience in mind from the start, not adapting them after the fact. A keynote can run live in the room and stream out simultaneously, followed by a virtual-only Q&A that gives remote attendees a moment that’s built just for them.


**Team Tip:** Assign one person on the production team whose only job is watching the stream as a virtual attendee would see it. Something that looks fine from the stage, like a slide that’s too small or audio that’s slightly off, often only shows up when someone is watching through a screen.


### **6. Build Your Event Team**


Split the team into two functional groups: one focused on the physical room, one focused on the virtual production. Trying to run both from a single team usually means someone gets stretched too thin right when the event starts. The in-person team handles registration, ushering, and AV; the virtual team handles streaming, moderation, and tech support for remote attendees.


Set a recurring check-in with both teams through the planning process so nobody is out of sync on last-minute changes.


### **7. Handle In-Person and Virtual Production**


On the physical side, confirm the venue has strong internet connectivity and enough power and space for cameras, lighting, and streaming equipment. Professional AV support is worth the cost for anything beyond a small internal meeting. On the virtual side, plan for streaming redundancy: a backup internet connection and a standby plan if the primary stream drops mid-session.


[Badge printing and check-in](https://inevent.com/en/pass-event-quick-checkin.php) tools speed up the in-person arrival experience and free up staff to help attendees rather than manage lines, which matters more the larger the in-person crowd gets.


### **8. Drive Engagement on Both Sides**


In-person engagement comes from the room itself: dedicated networking time, workshops, and panel discussions. Virtual engagement needs to be built deliberately, since remote attendees can’t just bump into someone at the coffee station. Breakout rooms, live polls, and


**[networking and AI matchmaking](https://inevent.com/en/event-management-software.php)** tools give virtual attendees a way to connect with the right people instead of just watching passively.


Event professionals back this up: as


[BizBash reports](https://www.bizbash.com/corporate-events/hybrid-meetings-continue-to-provide-a-relevant-and-effective-tool-in-2021) , one hotel events director recommends coordinating smaller breakout sessions specifically so virtual attendees can connect with each other one-on-one, rather than just watching a stream.


### **9. Build a Hybrid Event Marketing Plan for Both Audiences**


Hybrid event marketing means selling two different experiences at once, and the messaging should say so directly: what someone gets by showing up in person, and what someone gets by joining remotely. Email campaigns should segment by likely attendance type where possible. Social media can promote behind-the-scenes content before the event and live moments during it. A


**[related blog post on promoting events for free](https://inevent.com/blog/marketing/ways-to-promote-your-event-for-free.html)** covers additional channels worth testing.


Traditional channels still have a place too, direct mail for high-value invitees, and partnerships with industry voices who can vouch for the event to their own audience.


For deeper channel-by-channel tactics,


**[HubSpot’s event marketing resources](https://www.hubspot.com/resources/event-marketing)** cover multi-channel campaign structures in more depth.


#### **10. Set Up Registration and Ticketing**


Offer separate ticket types for in-person and virtual attendance, and be specific about what each one includes. A clear


**[event registration process](https://inevent.com/blog/others/event-registration-tips-to-gain-attendees.html)** reduces drop-off, and the data collected at registration should feed directly into how sessions and follow-ups get personalized later.


### **11. Manage Event Day Operations**


On event day, in-person staff need clear roles and a fast


**[check-in](https://inevent.com/blog/others/3-check-in-solutions-you-need-for-safe-hybrid-events.html)** process so lines don’t build up at the door. Virtual operations need a standing tech-support presence and active moderation, since problems in a live chat can spiral fast if nobody is watching it.


### **12. Follow Up and Measure Results**


The event isn’t finished when the last session ends. Send


**[post-event surveys](https://inevent.com/blog/others/15-post-event-survey-questions-for-attendees.html)** to both audiences, since in-person and virtual attendees often have different feedback. Make recordings and on-demand content available quickly while the event is still fresh in people’s minds, and compare turnout and engagement numbers against the goals set in step one.


In our platform data, events that send a follow-up survey within 48 hours see meaningfully higher response rates than those that wait a week or more.


##


**Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What is the difference between a hybrid event and a virtual event?**


A hybrid event includes both an in-person audience and a virtual audience attending the same live event, while a virtual event has no physical venue at all. Hybrid events need in-person logistics like venue and catering on top of the virtual production a fully online event would need.


### **How much does a hybrid event cost?**


Hybrid event costs vary widely based on venue size, streaming quality, and staffing, but organizers should budget separately for in-person costs (venue, AV, catering) and virtual costs (streaming platform, technical support). Building both budgets early, with a 10-15% contingency buffer, prevents surprises later in planning.


### **What equipment do you need for a hybrid event?**


A hybrid event needs reliable in-person AV equipment (cameras, microphones, and lighting) plus a stable internet connection with backup, a streaming platform, and a way to manage two-way interaction like chat or Q&A for remote attendees. Venue internet strength is often the most overlooked requirement.


### **How do you keep virtual attendees engaged during a hybrid event?**


Virtual attendees stay engaged through breakout rooms, live polls, dedicated virtual Q&A moments, and networking tools built for remote interaction. InEvent event strategists recommend giving virtual attendees at least one interaction point per session, rather than leaving them to passively watch a stream.


### **What is the best platform for hosting a hybrid event?**


The best hybrid event platform depends on the event’s size and goals, but it should combine registration, streaming, and engagement tools in one system rather than requiring separate logins for each. Full feature and pricing details for InEvent’s platform are available on the

##


**Conclusion**


A hybrid event succeeds when the in-person and virtual experiences get equal planning attention, not when one gets treated as the main event and the other as an afterthought. Working through this hybrid event checklist step by step, from goals through follow-up, catches the gaps that usually only show up once it’s too late to fix them.
